source.title: How Much More Data Do I Need? Estimating Requirements for Downstream Tasks
source.authors: Rafid Mahmood; James Lucas; David Acuna; Daiqing Li; Jonah Philion; J. M. Álvarez; Zhi-Ding Yu; Sania Fidler; M. Law

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates power-law performance extrapolation on computer-vision tasks, extending the question to image models and data-size scaling rather than language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The study's own results measure extrapolation of image-model accuracy, AP, and IoU as training data size increases. It does not test language models, held-out pretraining loss, parameter-count or compute scaling, or a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Its discussion of language-model scaling laws and cited results from other work are not recorded as findings.
record.test_reason: The study fits a power law (with offset) and three saturating alternatives to vision task scores against training-set size, then measures extrapolation error. Its own results show the power law is often not the best-fitting form: Arctan beats it on all classification sets and other forms beat it elsewhere. That bears on whether the power-law form carries over to other modalities (V5) and on how much functional-form and fitting choices matter (V7). Caveats: the measure is accuracy, AP or IoU rather than loss; only data size varies; and extrapolation spans at most 10x (10% to 100% of the data).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also find that saturating alternatives (notably Arctan) often extrapolate scores more accurately than the power law. Even so, lower regression error does not yield better data-requirement estimates. Small score errors cause large data mis-estimates, and a correction factor plus up to five collection rounds works best.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits candidate curves to computer-vision task scores against training dataset size and evaluates extrapolation; it does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy against parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Extrapolation errors vary with initial dataset fraction, dataset/task, and regression-function choice. The study also reports that ground-truth score curves for some settings are not always concave and monotonically increasing.

fits_no_version.finding: Small errors in extrapolated score produce large errors in the estimated data requirement. On ImageNet, a 1-6% score error leads to missing the requirement by 120k-310k images.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Accuracy of scaling-law extrapolation is insufficient for inverting the curve to estimate the data needed to reach a target.

record.problems: The study evaluates a simulation using a preconstructed piecewise-linear ground-truth score curve rather than repeatedly collecting data, training, and evaluating during each simulated round; the authors note that simulation quality depends on the number of subsets used to construct that curve. It evaluates image task metrics, not language-model loss.
record.rows_left_out: The 20% initial-data rows for CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet, nuScenes detection, BDD100K, and nuScenes BEV segmentation from Table 3 are omitted to retain comparisons at the small and large initial-data settings within the 60-row limit. Also omitted are Table 4 and Figures 3–5 data-collection simulation ratios, Table 5 signed regression-error values, Table 6 architecture ablations, and Appendix Figures 8–9; these examine data-requirement simulations, alternate error metrics, architectures, class-specific scores, and active learning rather than additional direct tests of power-law score extrapolation retained here.

untested.parts: Language-model pretraining loss; parameters and compute; not tested at all.
Language-model loss extrapolation across orders of magnitude. Vision extrapolation here spans at most 10x in data and uses task scores.
Loss at fixed parameter count across shapes. The Table 6 depth and width ablations report extrapolation RMSE only.
Loss as the measure; model-size and compute scaling; video and other modalities; repeated data; fine-tuning and transfer. Only data size versus accuracy, AP or IoU in supervised vision is tested.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining scale or loss; not studied.
Fitted language-model exponents, parameter counting and the compute-optimal split are not tested.

missing.what: Optimistic/pessimistic ranking of fits: the power law is among the two most pessimistic fits in 0/21 regression plots, while Arctan is in 19/21. The power law consistently overpredicts score at larger data sizes.
Ground-truth score-versus-data curves for VOC and BDD100K are not always concave or monotonically increasing. Some nuScenes class-specific AP values decrease with more data.

record.verdict_notes: The rows measure vision task scores (not loss) against data size only, extrapolating at most 10x. This weakens their bearing on V5's loss-based power-law form. Comparator rows for non-power-law functions cannot speak to V5 alone, so they are relinked to V7 as cannot_determine. The declared omissions (the 20% rows, Table 6 with ResNet50 power-law RMSE of 276 at 10%, and Table 5) would strengthen the V5 limits_scope verdicts if added.

versions.untested_parts: It measures computer-vision task scores rather than held-out language-model pretraining loss, and does not vary parameters or compute.
It evaluates estimates of computer-vision scores from smaller data subsets, not loss predictions for language-model runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameter count and training tokens is studied.
The architecture ablations report extrapolation errors, not loss comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Tests image-model task scores as a function of dataset size; does not test other modalities, language-model pretraining loss, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Does not study downstream language-model task performance or its relationship to pretraining loss.

Shows dependence on regression-function choice and initial data fraction, and discusses some curves that are not concave and monotonically increasing. Does not test fitted language-model exponents or compute-optimal allocation.

relationships.condition: Classification (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet) at both 10% and 50% initial data
relationships.reason: The power law extrapolates accuracy markedly worse than a saturating Arctan: RMSE 39.0/34.4/23.9 at 10% and 6.0/5.5/5.1 at 50%, against Arctan's 8.0/13.3/3.2 and 0.38/0.69/0.74 (T3-C10-10-PL, T3-C100-10-PL, T3-IN-10-PL, T3-C10-50-PL, T3-C100-50-PL, T3-IN-50-PL).
relationships.display_finding: Across CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and ImageNet, power-law RMSE was 39.0/34.4/23.9 at 10% initial data and 6.0/5.5/5.1 at 50%, versus Arctan's 8.0/13.3/3.2 and 0.38/0.69/0.74.

source_check.reason: Table 3 confirms all stated comparisons. Arctan consistently outperforms Power Law, qualifying its accuracy without establishing an absent scaling effect; the authors still describe all 50% fits as low-error.

relationships.condition: Detection and segmentation with small initial data (10%, or 20% for VOC)
relationships.reason: Power-law RMSE is 4.66, 6.57, 9.85 and 2.78 (T3-VOC-20-PL, T3-NSD-10-PL, T3-BDD-10-PL, T3-NSB-10-PL). Most functions diverge from the ground truth, and an alternative form beats the power law in each case.
relationships.display_finding: Power-law RMSE values were 4.66, 6.57, 9.85 and 2.78 across the detection and segmentation cases; alternative functions performed better in every case, although most functions diverged from measured performance.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Detection and segmentation with small initial data (10%, or 20% for VOC)
source_check.reason: Table 3 confirms Power Law RMSE 4.66, 6.57, 9.85 and 2.78, with a better alternative in every setting. Section 4.2 identifies small-data extrapolation as unreliable.

relationships.condition: Detection and segmentation with 50% initial data
relationships.reason: Power-law extrapolation RMSE is low at 1.15, 0.69, 1.30 and 0.38 (T3-VOC-50-PL, T3-NSD-50-PL, T3-BDD-50-PL, T3-NSB-50-PL), comparable to the alternatives. This holds over only a 2x extrapolation and on task scores.
relationships.display_finding: Power-law extrapolation achieved RMSE values of 1.15, 0.69, 1.30, and 0.38 on task scores, comparable to alternatives over a twofold extrapolation.

relationships.condition: Choice of functional form and amount of fitting data, across all vision tasks
relationships.reason: Extrapolation error depends strongly on the fitted form and the initial fraction, with no uniformly best function (e.g. T3-C10-10-PL 39.0 vs T3-C10-10-A 7.98; T3-NSD-10-PL 6.57 vs T3-NSD-10-L 0.79). The text adds that the power law is never among the most pessimistic fits (0/21), so it systematically overpredicts.
relationships.display_finding: Extrapolation error depends strongly on functional form and initial data fraction, with power-law errors of 39.0 and 6.57 versus alternatives' 7.98 and 0.79 and no uniformly best function; power laws are among the most pessimistic fits in 0 of 21 comparisons.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Choice of functional form and amount of fitting data, across all vision tasks
source_check.reason: Table 3 supports sensitivity to functional form and fitting-data fraction. Appendix B reports Power Law among the two most pessimistic estimators in 0/21 plots and calls it generally optimistic; this does not mean it always overpredicts.
